title: New Skate Park Opens in Santo Domingo
paragraphs: A new skate park opened last weekend in Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic. More than four hundred young people came to the opening, and many of them stayed until night.

The park was built in an old car park behind the National Library. It has two bowls, a long rail and a small area for beginners. The project cost nine million pesos, and it was paid for by the city and by a sports brand.

Skater Yamilet Peña, nineteen, said, 'Before this park, we used to skate in the streets, and the police sometimes stopped us. It was dangerous because of the cars. Now we have a safe place, and it's free.'
The park is open every day from 8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. Helmets and knee pads are compulsory. There are also free lessons every Saturday at four o'clock for people who have never skated before.
Next year, the city is planning to build two more parks in other areas.

title: My Week Without Sugar
paragraphs: Monday. Today I started my week without sugar. My doctor says I eat too many sweet things, and I agree. This morning I had bread with cheese and a coffee without sugar. It tasted terrible!

Tuesday. I was really tired and in a bad mood. At lunchtime I saw a chocolate cake at the cafeteria, and I almost bought it. Instead, I ate an apple. A friend laughed at me, but she also wanted to try the challenge.

Wednesday. I read the labels of all the food in my kitchen, and I was shocked. Even the tomato sauce has sugar! There are two spoons of sugar in a small bottle of orange juice. Now I understand why I always feel hungry in the afternoon.
Thursday. It was easier today. I wasn't thinking about sweets all the time, and I had more energy at football practice. Fruit tastes sweeter than before. Is that possible?
Sunday. I did it! Seven days without sugar. I'm not going to stop completely, because I love my grandmother's cake. But from now on, I'm going to eat sweet things only at the weekend.

title: A Suitcase That Never Arrived
paragraphs: Dear Customer Service,
I'm writing about my flight from Lima to Madrid on 3 March. Unfortunately, my suitcase didn't arrive with me, and I need your help.

I waited at the baggage belt for one hour. Then I went to the lost luggage desk, and a worker gave me a form. She said they were going to find my bag in two days. It's now been six days, and I haven't received any news.

The suitcase is blue and medium-sized. It has a red ribbon on the handle. Inside, there are my work clothes, a pair of shoes and some important documents. I'm here for a job interview, and I had to buy a new shirt for 35 euros.
Please tell me where my suitcase is. I would also like you to pay for the shirt. I'm sending you a photo of the receipt. Please reply as soon as possible.
Yours faithfully,
Andrea Núñez

title: Tea or Coffee Around the World
paragraphs: In many countries, people start the day with a hot drink. But which drink is more popular: tea or coffee? The answer depends on where you live.

In Colombia and Brazil, coffee is more popular than tea. These two countries grow a lot of coffee, and people drink it in small cups at home, at work and on the street. In Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, however, the favourite drink is mate. People share it with friends and family, and they pass it from one person to the next.
In the United Kingdom and Ireland, tea is more popular than coffee. The average person in Ireland drinks about four cups of tea a day. They usually add a little milk and sometimes a spoon of sugar.
In Japan and China, people prefer green tea. It doesn't have as much caffeine as coffee, and many families drink it after every meal.

Both drinks are good if you don't drink too much. Doctors say that three or four cups of coffee a day is the maximum for most adults. After that, you may feel nervous and sleep badly. So next time, think about which drink you really need.

title: Carolina: Football Before Breakfast
paragraphs: Carolina Rúa is eighteen and plays football for a club in Medellín. Last month she joined the national youth team. We spoke to her after training.
Interviewer: When did you start playing?
Carolina: When I was nine. My cousins used to play in the street, and one day they let me join. I scored two goals, and they never said no again!
Interviewer: What does a normal day look like?
Carolina: I get up at five-thirty and go to training from six to eight. Then I go to school until two. In the afternoon I do my homework and rest. I go to bed at nine.
Interviewer: Is it expensive to play?
Carolina: The club pays for my shoes and my bus ticket, but my parents pay for my food and clothes. A good pair of shoes costs about 300,000 pesos, so I take care of them.
Interviewer: What are your dreams?
Carolina: I want to play in Europe one day. First, I need to improve my English, because a lot of coaches speak it. That's why I'm studying with an app every evening.

title: The Note in the Library Book
paragraphs: Irene was studying for her exams in the university library in Valencia when she opened an old book about history. A small piece of paper fell out. On it, somebody had written in blue ink: 'Meet me under the clock at five o'clock. Bring the red umbrella.'

Irene looked at the date in the book. It was last borrowed many years ago. 'Who wrote this?' she thought. 'Did the two people meet?' She was curious, so she asked the librarian. The librarian smiled and said, 'I don't know, but the book was borrowed by a man called Tomás.'

That evening, Irene went to the old clock in the central square. She didn't bring an umbrella, but she waited. At ten past five, an old man with a red umbrella walked past. 'Excuse me,' said Irene. 'Are you Tomás?'

He was surprised. 'Yes! How do you know my name?' Irene showed him the note, and he started to laugh. 'I wrote this for my wife a long time ago. We met under that clock, and we're still married. I used it as a bookmark and forgot about it.'
'Thank you for bringing back this memory,' he said. 'Would you like a coffee?' They sat in a café for an hour, and he told her the whole story.

title: Six Months with My First Guitar
paragraphs: Six months ago my uncle gave me an old guitar. I'm twenty, and I've never played any instrument before, so I decided to learn from videos on the internet. This is my story so far.

At the beginning, my fingers hurt a lot. I practised every day for twenty minutes, but I couldn't play a single song. The chords were difficult, and the sound was terrible. My neighbours probably hated me!
After one month, I learned three simple chords: G, C and D. With these chords, you can play hundreds of songs. My first song was very slow, but my flatmate clapped at the end.

The internet has many free videos, but not all of them are good. I follow a teacher from Argentina who explains everything step by step. He says that it's better to practise a little every day than to practise for three hours on Sunday. He's right!
Next month, I'm going to buy a new set of strings, because the old ones sound dull. I'm also going to play at an open-mic night in a café in Bogotá. I'm terrified, but I want to try. Wish me luck!

title: Weekend Courses at Greenfield Community Centre
paragraphs: Greenfield Community Centre, Dublin – Weekend Courses
Do you want to learn something new? This autumn, we offer four weekend courses for people aged sixteen and over. All our teachers are local people with years of experience.
Photography (Saturdays, 10:00–12:00): Learn to take better photos with your phone or a camera. Price: 60 euros for six weeks.
Cooking for Beginners (Saturdays, 2:00–4:30): Make simple, healthy meals that cost less than five euros a portion. You take your food home. Price: 80 euros, including ingredients.
Spanish for Travellers (Sundays, 11:00–12:30): Learn useful words and phrases for your next holiday. Price: 50 euros.
Bike Repair (Sundays, 2:00–4:00): Fix a flat tyre, change a chain and keep your bike in good condition. Bring your own bike. Price: 40 euros.
How to book: Come to the reception desk or call 01 555 0198. Places are limited to twelve people in each course, so book early. If you cancel one week before, we return your money.

title: How to Fix a Flat Bike Tyre
paragraphs: A flat tyre is a common problem for people who ride a bike every day. You don't need a mechanic. With a few tools, you can fix it in about twenty minutes. Here's how.
You need: a pump, two tyre levers, a new inner tube and a clean cloth.
Step 1: Turn the bike upside down and take off the wheel. If the wheel has a quick-release lever, open it. If not, use a spanner to open the nuts.
Step 2: Let the air out of the tyre. Then put the tyre levers between the tyre and the wheel and push them down. One side of the tyre comes off.

Step 3: Pull out the old inner tube. Check the inside of the tyre carefully with your fingers. If you find a sharp stone or a small piece of glass, remove it. Otherwise, the new tube will go flat again.
Step 4: Put in the new inner tube with a little air inside. Then push the tyre back onto the wheel, pump it up and put the wheel back on the bike.
Tip: Always carry a small pump and a spare tube when you ride. Check the tyre pressure once a week.

title: Luna Verde Live in Santiago
paragraphs: Last Saturday, I went to see my favourite band, Luna Verde, with two friends from university. We bought the tickets two months before, and they cost 35,000 pesos each. We arrived at six o'clock, but the concert started at nine, so we waited in a long line.

The band played for two hours, and the singer, Marta, was incredible. Her voice was stronger than on the records. They played all their famous songs and four new ones. During the slow song 'Mar', everybody turned on their phone lights, and the field looked like a sky full of stars.

However, there were some problems. The sound was too loud near the stage, and I couldn't hear the words. The drinks were expensive: a small bottle of water cost 3,000 pesos! And when the concert finished, there were not enough buses, so we walked home for forty minutes.
Was it worth it? Definitely. It was the best night of the year. I give it four stars out of five because of the sound and the prices. If you get the chance to see them, go!
